query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (~5 at.%) of chromium to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its resistance to oxygen attack by promoting the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent CrTaO4‐based oxide layer that retards oxygen diffusion into the bulk.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr as produced, exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with poor oxygen resistance under high-temperature air exposure.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by incorporating approximately 5 at.% Cr (via substitution of a similar fraction of an existing element, e.g., Nb) to yield a Cr-containing variant of HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at temperatures between 800 °C and 1000 °C. Exposure durations from 5 hours (initial screening) up to 100 hours. Mechanical performance to be evaluated under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹, consistent with prior tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a surface oxide layer primarily consisting of CrTaO4.
generation.mechanism: The introduced Cr preferentially oxidizes in the presence of Ta to form a CrTaO4 layer. This layer is dense and adherent, acting as a barrier that slows oxygen ingress and minimizes further oxidative degradation, all while not substantially altering the alloy’s favorable mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the Cr-modified alloy should show a significantly lower oxidation weight gain, fewer scale spallation events, and maintain similar room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits significant oxidation under high-temperature air exposure (e.g., pest oxidation phenomena observed at around 800 °C) which precludes its use in high-temperature applications despite its acceptable mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The expected benefit is valid under oxidizing atmospheres (air) in the temperature range of 800–1000 °C for exposures from 5 to 100 hours; mechanical loading conditions remain consistent with those previously validated, ensuring that modifications do not significantly impair tensile ductility or yield strength.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal Cr concentration and its impact on phase stability and mechanical properties require further investigation. The interplay between Cr addition and the formation kinetics of CrTaO4 may also depend on subtle microstructural factors not yet fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy (control) and (2) a modified alloy with ~5 at.% Cr substituted into the composition. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation in air at 800 °C for an initial period of 5 hours, with optional extended tests up to 100 hours. Characterize the oxide scale by measuring weight gain, performing microscopic (SEM/TEM) and XRD analyses to verify the presence and continuity of the CrTaO4 phase, and assess any spallation. Additionally, measure the room- and high-temperature mechanical properties to confirm that ductility and yield strength remain within acceptable ranges.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and phase composition (via SEM, TEM, and XRD)
Mechanical properties: room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-added alloy fails to exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain, does not form a continuous, adherent CrTaO4 oxide layer, or if its mechanical properties degrade beyond acceptable limits compared to the control alloy, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

At 1100 oC, NV1 alloy outperformed all 3 other alloys (AlCrMoNbTi, (AlCrMoNbTi)0.99Si0.01, and AlCrMoTaTi) within 48 hours. The main difference in the composition of NV1 alloy was 75% less Ti comparing to AlCrMoNbTi, (AlCrMoNbTi)0.99Si0.01, and AlCrMoTaTi. Since CrTaO4 layer played a major role in reducing the oxidation of NV1 alloy, it is very likely that the reduced Ti content of NV1 alloy promoted the formation of CrTaO4 layer, leading to enhanced oxidation resistance at 1100 °C. In summary, isothermal oxidation at 1000 and 1100 °C was performed on a novel RHEA for up to 200 hours, such long-term oxidation test has not been reported before for this class of alloys. The weight gain behaviours during the tests could be affected by evolutions of external oxidation, internal oxidation, and nitridation. The multiple stages of weight gain behaviour at 1100 °C were never discussed in previous studies since most of them only presented the results of oxidation up to 48 hours,. We believe that CrTaO4-based protection layer and Si addition may be important for future development of RHEA against oxidation and nitridation. However, it is also possible that the growth of a protective Al2O3 or Cr2O3 layer was hindered by prominent CrTaO4-based oxide presence. In both cases, the nature of such CrTaO4-based oxide needs to be carefully examined in the future studies of RHEAs.
